lessons.title: What an animal health system is
lessons.html:
From treating sick animals to managing herd health

An animal health system is the planned set of actions a farm uses to prevent, detect and control disease. Treating a sick heifer is part of it, but the real value lies in prevention: vaccination, parasite control, biosecurity, nutrition, hygiene and good records. Evaluating the system means checking whether it actually keeps animals healthy and productive at a sensible cost.

Building blocks of a herd health plan

  • Vaccination programme drawn up with your vet for local risks, for example anthrax, botulism, blackquarter, lumpy skin disease, Rift Valley fever or enterotoxaemia, depending on area and species.
  • Internal and external parasite control: ticks, flies, roundworms such as wireworm, liver fluke where present.
  • Biosecurity: control of animals, people and vehicles coming onto the farm.
  • Nutrition and water: poorly fed animals have weak immunity.
  • Records: treatments, deaths, abortions, weights and production.

Legal duties

The Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 deals with controlled and notifiable diseases. Suspected cases of diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease must be reported to the state veterinarian, and movement restrictions or official control measures must be followed. Stock remedies are registered under Act 36 of 1947; use them only according to the label or a veterinary prescription.

A health plan is written for a specific farm. A Highveld dairy, a Karoo sheep farm and a Limpopo game-and-cattle operation face very different disease risks, so do not copy a neighbour's plan without checking it with a vet.

lessons.title: Measuring health performance
lessons.html:
Using records to evaluate the system

You cannot evaluate what you do not measure. Simple, consistent records reveal whether the health system is working.

IndicatorWhat it tells you
Mortality rate by age groupLosses in calves, weaners or adults
Calving or lambing percentageFertility, abortion and neonatal losses
Weaning weightCombined effect of milk, health and parasites
Treatment cases per 100 animalsDisease pressure and treatment cost
Mastitis and cell count (dairy)Udder health and milking hygiene
Faecal egg counts or FAMACHA scores (small stock)Worm burden and need to dose

Analysing the numbers

Compare results over time, between camps and with targets agreed with your vet or industry benchmarks. Look for patterns: deaths clustered in a season, one camp with more abortions, or a rise in pneumonia after transport. Calculate the cost of disease, including lost production, not just medicine. For example, if a herd of 200 cows loses 10 extra calves a year and each weaner is worth about R6 000, the loss is around R60 000 before treatment costs.

Parasite resistance

Overuse of the same dewormer or dip has led to resistance on many SA farms. Targeted treatment (dosing only animals that need it, using FAMACHA in sheep and goats), rotating actives as advised, correct dosing to weight and checking efficacy with faecal egg counts all slow resistance. Evaluate whether your products still work instead of assuming they do.

Post-mortems

When animals die unexpectedly, ask a vet to do a post-mortem or take samples. Do not open carcasses of animals that died suddenly with bleeding from openings, because anthrax is possible and opening the carcass spreads spores and endangers people.

lessons.title: Biosecurity and improving the system
lessons.html:
Keeping disease out and improving continually

Biosecurity measures

  • Buy animals from known sources with health records; quarantine new arrivals in a separate camp before mixing.
  • Control visitor and vehicle access; provide footbaths or boot changes at animal houses.
  • Keep fences in good repair to prevent contact with neighbouring or wild animals where disease risk exists.
  • Dispose of carcasses properly and promptly.
  • Clean and disinfect equipment such as dosing guns, needles and ear-tag applicators.

Evaluating and improving

Use a simple cycle: plan (health plan with targets), do (carry out vaccinations and treatments on time), check (review records quarterly with your vet) and act (change what is not working). Questions to ask in a review:

  1. Were all vaccinations done on schedule and with correctly stored vaccines (cold chain)?
  2. Did losses fall, stay the same or rise?
  3. Are treatment costs per animal rising?
  4. Are staff trained to spot sick animals early and record treatments?
  5. Are residue withdrawal periods being respected before sale?

People and safety

Some animal diseases, such as brucellosis, anthrax, rabies and Rift Valley fever, can infect people. Wear gloves when handling aborted material, wash hands, never drink raw milk from untested herds and report suspected cases. Handle syringes with care and never recap needles by hand in a rush. Store remedies locked away from children and food.

Key points

  • Prevention through vaccination, parasite control, biosecurity and nutrition is the core of herd health.
  • Report suspected controlled diseases to the state vet as required by Act 35 of 1984.
  • Use records and indicators to measure whether the system works.
  • Check dewormer and dip effectiveness to manage resistance.
  • Protect people from zoonotic diseases.
